verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, of the sons of Korah, a mizmor.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the leader of the music. A song of the sons of Korah, to be sung with instruments.
verses.directors_commentary: In the Hebrew this heading is the first verse; the KJV counts it as verse 0 and starts at 'O clap your hands'. Every verse number in the psalm therefore shifts by one. 'Chief Musician' in the KJV is a guess at lamnatseach, a title whose root means 'to excel' or 'to oversee'. It points to a Temple music official who directed performance, which makes this a text for use in worship and not private prayer. mizmor is a song sung to stringed accompaniment, from the root zamar, which comes back five times in verses 7 and 8 (four in verse 7, once in verse 8). The Korahites were a family of Levitical singers, which is why the psalm sounds like a liturgy.

philological_notes.note: A performance title. The root means 'to be pre-eminent, to oversee', hence the 'overseer' of YLT and 'chief musician' of the KJV. The exact duty is not known.
A song sung to instruments. It shares its root with the repeated verb zamru in 47:7-8, so the heading names the act the psalm commands.

verses.translation_literal: All the peoples, strike [the] palm; shout to God with the voice of a ringing cry.
verses.translation_dramatic: All you peoples, every one: strike palm against palm. Lift your voices to God, and let the cry ring out.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens with an order, shouted at a crowd, and the crowd is 'all the peoples', not Israel. The KJV 'clap your hands' is close to the Hebrew but too tame. tiq'u kaf uses the verb for blowing a horn, pitching a tent peg and striking a hand against a hand, so this is a sharp slap, a gesture of joy (Metzudat Zion compares Nahum 3:19). The second command, hari'u, is the same word used for the war cry and for the shout that greets a new king. The KJV 'voice of triumph' for qol rinnah shifts the sense. Rinnah is a ringing cry of joy, and nothing in the word is military. Actors should treat the whole line as the noise of a coronation crowd. Malbim also links the shout to the crowning of a king.

philological_notes.note: The verb tq' means to strike or drive in, as with a horn blast or a tent peg. Here the object is the palm. Metzudat Zion defines it as striking one palm against another for joy and cites Nahum 3:19.
To raise a loud shout. It is used for war cries, for the greeting of a king and for joy, and the noun teru'ah in verse 6 comes from the same root. Malbim reads it here as the shout of enthronement.

verses.translation_literal: For YHWH Most High [is] fearsome, a great king over all the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the LORD is the Most High, and the awe of him is real. He is a great king, and the whole earth lies under his rule.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the reason for the shouting, and ki ('for') opens it. Two titles stand side by side: 'Most High' ('elyon) and 'great king'. 'Great king' was the formal title of the Near Eastern emperor, who held lesser kings as vassals, so a hearer in Jerusalem would have heard a claim that YHWH outranks every throne, and the nations in the audience would hear it too. The KJV 'terrible' is a good example of English drift. In 1611 it meant 'inspiring terror or awe', and it now means 'bad'. The Hebrew nora' is a passive form of the root for fear, 'one to be feared, awe-inspiring'. BBE's 'to be feared' is more accurate. Metzudat David reads the verse as the nations coming to know that God is above everything and awesome to them.

philological_notes.note: A niphal participle of the root 'to fear', meaning 'to be feared, awe-inspiring'. The KJV 'terrible' kept the older sense of the English word and now misleads.
'Most High', from the root 'to go up'. Used here as a title of YHWH, and it prepares the language of ascent in 47:6 and 47:10 (the verb 'alah).

verses.translation_literal: He subdues peoples under us, and nations under our feet.
verses.translation_dramatic: He brings peoples down beneath us, and the nations lie under our feet.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice shifts here from the shouted command to the speakers' own 'us', Israel. It is the hardest verse of the psalm for a modern audience, because the same peoples summoned to clap in verse 2 are now under Israel's feet. The Hebrew keeps both parts together, and an actor must hold them without softening either. Rashi and the Targum read yadber as dever, 'plague', so God sends plague on the idol-worshippers in Israel's place (Rashi compares Isaiah 43:3). Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as 'leads', as a flock is driven, and Radak adds that God leads the nations 'from the ends of the earth to Jerusalem'. That second reading fits what follows, where the nobles gather in verse 10. The KJV 'subdue' takes a side without telling you the root is disputed. 'Under our feet' is the picture of the conqueror's foot on the neck, which kings in the ancient Near East had carved on their monuments.

philological_notes.note: A hiphil of dbr II, 'to lead, drive' (as a shepherd drives a flock), hence 'subdue'. Rashi reads it from dever, 'plague', and the Targum follows him with 'he kills'.

verses.translation_literal: He chooses for us [obj] our inheritance, [obj] the pride of Jacob whom he loved. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: He chooses for us our inheritance, the pride of Jacob, whom he loved. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Inheritance' (nachalah) is a land word. In Israel a nachalah was the family plot passed from father to son, and it could not be sold for good, so to hear that God 'chooses' it is to hear the whole land as a gift that was given and not won. The commentators divide over the 'pride of Jacob'. Radak reads it as the land itself, 'the pride of Jacob and their glory', and takes 'whom he loved' as the place God loved, which is Jerusalem. Meiri, Metzudat David and the Targum read it as the Temple, and Meiri cites Psalm 87:2, 'the LORD loves the gates of Zion', to show that 'he loved' points back to God. The Hebrew ga'on is stronger than the KJV 'excellency'. It means 'swelling, majesty', and in the prophets it can be a boast (Amos 8:7). Here it names what Jacob is proud of. The final word Selah is a marker whose meaning is not known: perhaps a pause, a lifting of the voice or an instrument cue. Treat it as a held breath. The Targum reads the whole verse as God choosing the Temple, 'the house of the sanctuary of Jacob, whom he loved for ever'.

philological_notes.note: 'The pride of Jacob'. Metzudat Zion links ga'on to ga'avah, 'exaltation'. Radak reads it as the land (and 'whom he loved' as Jerusalem); Meiri, Metzudat David and the Targum read it as the Temple, which Meiri ties to Psalm 87:2.
A musical or liturgical marker of unknown meaning. It is left untranslated in the literal layer.

verses.translation_literal: God has gone up with a shout, YHWH with the sound of a ram's horn.
verses.translation_dramatic: God has gone up! The shout rises with him, and the ram's horn sounds, and the LORD is lifted on its call.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the center of the psalm, and it is a procession: God 'goes up', most likely into the Temple on its hill, with a crowd shouting (teru'ah) and the shofar blowing. The KJV 'trumpet' is a mistranslation. A shofar is a ram's horn, a single-note signal instrument with a harsh, rough sound, and it was blown at a king's accession and at festivals. A trumpet of the English kind, a metal instrument, is the chatzotzerah, a different word. So the sound is raw and loud, not brassy. The verse also uses two divine names in parallel, Elohim and YHWH. Malbim reads the two as two kinds of rule, nature and miracle, but the parallelism is the simpler explanation. Ibn Ezra reads the verse as an ascent of the Ark, and others as the Temple. The Hebrew does not say where he goes up, and the director should not choose.

philological_notes.note: 'He has gone up'. In the Jerusalem setting it is the verb of pilgrimage and procession, and it picks up 'Most High' ('elyon) in verse 3 and na'alah in verse 10. Ibn Ezra connects the verb with the Ark.
A ram's horn, not a metal trumpet. The KJV 'trumpet' blurs it with the chatzotzerah.

verses.translation_literal: Sing praises [to] God, sing praises; sing praises to our king, sing praises.
verses.translation_dramatic: Sing! Sing to God, sing. Sing to our king, and sing again.
verses.directors_commentary: Four times in one line the Hebrew says zamru, 'make music'. The KJV and ASV keep the repetition, but YLT's 'Praise God--praise--give praise' shows how it breaks up when it is varied. It drives like a drum beat, and the actors should say it that way, each zamru heavier than the last. Radak says the doubling is for emphasis, and Metzudat David that it is for continuance. The shift from 'God' to 'our king' narrows the focus: Israel's own king, whom the first half of the psalm had made king of all the earth. Radak reads 'our king' as a statement that for now God is king over Israel in a special way, and that on the day the psalm has in view he will be king of all.

philological_notes.note: To make music to an instrument, to sing praise. It appears four times in this verse, and a fifth time in verse 8, and the same root gives the mizmor of the heading.

verses.translation_literal: For [the] king of all the earth [is] God; sing praises, a maskil.
verses.translation_dramatic: For God is king of all the earth. Sing, and sing with understanding.
verses.directors_commentary: The ground for the singing returns in a different order from verse 3: 'king of all the earth, God', with the king placed first for stress. It is the psalm's whole claim in seven words. The last word, maskil, is the hard one. It is a heading in other psalms, where it names a type of poem, and here it stands inside the verse, after the command to sing. The KJV 'with understanding' and the Targum 'with good understanding' take it as an adverb. Meiri and Metzudat David read it as 'a song made with insight', a song that gives the hearers something to understand and not only a crowd's noise. YLT 'O understanding one' takes it as an address to the singer, and Radak reads it as an address to the wise among Israel and the nations. The Hebrew allows each of these, and an actor can choose one. The root is skl, 'to have insight', which in this psalm sets the thoughtful song against the shout of verse 2.

philological_notes.note: From the root 'to have insight, to act wisely'. In other psalm headings it labels a kind of poem. Here it follows 'sing praises' and can be adverbial ('with understanding'), a noun ('a maskil') or an address ('O wise one'). The commentators in the packet split between these.

token_glosses.gloss: a maskil, a song of insight

verses.translation_literal: God reigns over nations; God sits on [the] throne of his holiness.
verses.translation_dramatic: God reigns over the nations. God has taken his seat upon his holy throne.
verses.directors_commentary: The perfect tense malak 'elohim is the old enthronement cry, 'God has become king' or 'God reigns', and it is said like the shout 'The king is dead, long live the king', as an event. The KJV's 'reigneth' is correct but flattens this into a general truth. Both 'reigns' and 'sits' are in the perfect, so the picture is that of a king who has just taken his throne. The KJV 'the heathen' for goyim is an old English word choice that reads as contempt; the Hebrew is the ordinary word for 'nations' and carries none. 'Throne of his holiness' is a Hebrew construction that the KJV keeps, and the ASV 'his holy throne' smooths it. Rashi, citing the Pesikta Rabbati, takes it that the throne is now 'whole and in recognised greatness'. The Targum has 'the throne of his sanctity'. The line is the end of the psalm's procession: God has gone up (verse 6) and is now seated.

philological_notes.note: A verb-first clause with the perfect tense, the form of an enthronement proclamation: 'God has become king / reigns'. The formula 'YHWH has become king' recurs in other psalms (93, 97, 99).
'The throne of his holiness', a construct chain. Malbim reads it as a throne above nature, in the realm of miracle, and Metzudat David as showing his rule over all.

verses.translation_literal: [The] nobles of [the] peoples are gathered, [the] people of [the] God of Abraham; for to God [belong] [the] shields of [the] earth; he is greatly exalted.
verses.translation_dramatic: The nobles of the peoples have gathered in, to stand as the people of Abraham's God. For the shields of the earth belong to God, and he is lifted high, and higher.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm ends with a scene, and it is a scene of the nations coming in, which is a surprise after the 'under our feet' of verse 4. The nedivim are nobles in the sense of 'the willing, the generous', from the root ndv, 'to give freely', so these are rulers who come of their own will. Metzudat Zion says a nadiv is one who is generous with money. Rashi reads the nedivim as those who offered themselves to be killed for the sanctification of God's name, and names Abraham, 'the first of the willing-hearted', as the first of the converts; Malbim is the one who reads the nobles themselves as converts who volunteered to join. The Hebrew does not say 'with' or 'as' before 'the people of the God of Abraham'. The ASV 'to be the people' and the YLT/BBE 'with' both add a word, so the director must choose. The speaker names Abraham and not Moses or David, and Abraham is the ancestor of many nations, the man through whom 'all the families of the earth' were to be blessed (Genesis 12:3). Radak and Meiri give the reason in the text's own terms: Abraham was the first to proclaim God's name in the world. 'Shields of the earth' (maginnei 'eretz) means the rulers, who protect their peoples as a shield does (Ibn Ezra, Radak). The KJV 'belong unto God' is correct, and its 'he is greatly exalted' echoes na'alah, which goes back to 'elyon in verse 3 and 'alah in verse 6, so the verb of ascent closes the psalm as it opened it.

philological_notes.note: 'Nobles of peoples', literally the willing or generous ones. Metzudat Zion says a nadiv is a man generous with wealth. Rashi reads it as those who offered themselves to be killed for the sanctification of God's name, and Malbim as nobles who volunteered to convert.

No preposition links this phrase to the verb: 'with' and 'as' are both possible. Radak and Meiri read it as the nobles becoming the people of Abraham's God, because Abraham was the first to proclaim God's name.
'Shields of the earth', meaning its rulers, who protect their people. Meiri compares Hosea 4:18, where the same word is used for leaders.
